notes.claim: Cutting every slice into 2 gives twice as many slices, and you then need twice as many of them for the same amount; multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number does not change what the fraction represents.
Equivalent fractions are made by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
Equivalent fractions name the same number: they sit at the same point on the number line.
A rational number can be thought of as a whole family of equivalent fractions, all at the same point on the number line.
Converting to equivalent fractions by multiplying top and bottom by the same number keeps the value of each fraction the same.

sources.title: An Introduction to Irrational Numbers | NRICH
sources.quote: They occupy the same point on the number line. In a sense, a rational number (the actual ratio) consists of a whole family of equivalent fractions.

sources.title: Equivalent fractions (video) | Khan Academy
sources.quote: If I multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number, then I'm not changing what that fraction represents.

sources.title: Equivalent fractions (video) | Khan Academy
sources.quote: Going from 4 slices to 8 slices, I cut every slice, I turned every slice into 2 more slices, so I had twice as many slices.

sources.title: Visualizing equivalent fractions review (article) | Khan Academy
sources.quote: Numbers are equivalent when they are located at the same point on the number line.

sources.title: Equivalent Fractions
sources.quote: Because when we multiply or divide both the top and bottom by the same number, the fraction keeps its value

sources.title: How to find equivalent fractions - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: Multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the same number.

sources.title: Common Denominator
sources.quote: We multiplied the top and bottom of each fraction by the denominator of the other: this keeps the value of the fraction the same!
